summary: Inheritance lets a subclass absorb a superclass's attributes and methods and add new ones. It models an **is-a** relationship and gives code reuse. The root of every Java class is `java.lang.Object`.
`super(...)` calls the superclass constructor and must be the **first statement** of the constructor. `super.m()` calls the superclass version of a method.

Overloading means the same name with a different parameter list (number or types). Overriding means the same signature and return type in a subclass, done either as **Refinement** (uses `super`) or as **Replacement**.
There are 4 access levels: public, protected (`#`), package/default (nothing written), private. `protected` = the class itself + subclasses + the same package.
`final` method = cannot be overridden. `final` class = cannot be extended. An abstract class cannot be instantiated, and its abstract methods have no body.
Java has single class inheritance but lets a class implement multiple interfaces. An interface can `extends` another interface.
mustMemorise: Overloading = same name, different **number** OR **types** of parameters. Return type or parameter names alone do NOT count.
Overriding = **exactly** the same signature and return type (per the slides). The 2 ways are **Refinement** (uses `super`) and **Replacement**.
`super()` must be the FIRST statement in a subclass constructor.
Method lookup starts at the class of the **object**, then goes up through each immediate superclass. If nothing matches, an error is reported.
Access table (Class / Package / Subclass / World): public YYYY, protected YYYN, default YYNN, private YNNN.
UML access symbols: `+` public, `#` protected, `-` private, `~` package.
`final` method: cannot be overridden. `final` class: cannot be a superclass, and its methods are implicitly final. Benefits: **security** and **efficiency** (compile-time binding).
Abstract in UML = name in *italics* OR the `{abstract}` constraint.
Interface (per the slides) = only abstract methods + constants (`static final`). A class implementing it must implement all of them or be declared abstract.
A class `extends` ONE class and `implements` MANY interfaces. Neither an abstract class nor an interface can be created with `new`.
Packages have a global namespace based on the internet domain (e.g. `sg.edu.ntu.projects`). No `package` line puts a class in the anonymous **default package**.

items.title: Definition of inheritance
notes: Inheritance derives new classes from existing ones by **absorbing** their attributes and behaviours AND **adding** new capabilities.
It gives code reuse and models an **is-a** relationship: a Student *is a* Person.
The root/ancestor of ALL Java classes is `java.lang.Object`.

items.title: Generalisation vs specialisation
notes: The superclass is a **generalisation** of its subclasses.
The subclasses are **specialisations** of the superclass.
In UML this is the generalisation relationship: a solid line with a hollow triangle pointing at the superclass.

items.title: Reading the Shape hierarchy
notes: A hollow-triangle arrow from Rectangle/Circle to Shape means `extends` (is-a). The arrowhead sits at the **superclass**.
Synonyms. Superclass: super / base / parent / generalised. Subclass: sub / derived / child / specialised.

The slide says subclasses inherit everything EXCEPT private members. Strictly, private fields still exist inside the subclass object but cannot be accessed by name, so `Rectangle` must use `getXPos()`.

items.title: Rectangle: super() constructor chaining
notes: `super(xCoor, yCoor)` must be the **first** statement in the constructor.
If you write no `super(...)` call, Java inserts `super()` (no arguments) automatically. That fails to compile if the superclass has no no-arg constructor.
`super.print()` inside `print()` reuses Shape's version. This is overriding by **refinement**.

items.title: The two uses of super
notes: 1) `super(args)` in a constructor calls the superclass constructor and must be the FIRST statement.
2) `super.method()` in any method calls the superclass's version of that method.
A subclass is declared with the `extends` keyword.

items.title: Methods inherited from the superclass
notes: `rect.getXPos()` compiles even though Rectangle doesn't declare it. It is inherited from Shape.
The search starts at Rectangle, finds nothing, then moves up to Shape (see slide 22).

items.title: Output typo: 'Width = 10'
notes: Line 2 shows `Width = 10`. `getWidth()` returns a `double`, so Java really prints `Width = 10.0` (checked on JDK 17).
Exam: for real output, always choose the `10.0` form.

items.title: Overloading rules
notes: Same method name but 1) a different **number** of parameters OR 2) different parameter **types**.
The slide says overloading is NOT a behaviour of inheritance. It is shown here only to compare with overriding.
Benefit: one name (`print(int)`, `print(String)`) instead of `printInt`, `printString`, and so on.

items.title: Crossed-out findMin(int a, int b, int c)
notes: Changing only the parameter **names** does not make a new signature. It is a compile error ('method already defined'), verified.
Changing only the **return type** is also not overloading, and is also a compile error.
The 3-arg version calls the 2-arg versions: min(min(a,b), min(b,c)) = the overall minimum.

items.title: Which overload is called
notes: `findMin(x,y)` with ints prints `10`. `findMin(i,j)` with doubles prints `4.5`. `findMin(x,y,z)` prints `5`.
The compiler picks the overload from the argument types at **compile time** (static binding, Ch5).

items.title: Overriding: the 2 ways
notes: To override, define a method with **exactly the same signature and return type** as the superclass method.
1) **Refinement**: reuse the superclass method via `super.method()` and add to it. 2) **Replacement**: rewrite the method completely.
Not on the slide but true in Java: the return type may be a subtype (covariant), and you cannot reduce visibility (e.g. public to default is a compile error).

items.title: Indirect inheritance (Disc to Circle to Shape)
notes: Disc extends Circle, which extends Shape. Disc **indirectly** inherits `getXPos()` and the other Shape members.
Each arrow goes only to the **immediate** superclass.

items.title: Disc: super.findArea() vs the overridden findArea()
notes: `super.findArea()` always runs **Circle's** version (πr²), so `findVolume` = πr²·t.
Trap: `super.print()` runs Circle's `print()`, but its call to `findArea()` is dynamically bound to **Disc's** `findArea()`.
So for `new Disc(10,20,5,10)` the 'Circle print' part prints `Area = 471.238...` (Disc's area), not 78.5 (verified).

items.title: DiscApp output (verified)
notes: `circ.print()` prints Center `[1.0, 5.0]`, Radius `10.0`, Area `314.159...`.
`disc.findVolume()` prints `785.398...` (= π·25·10).
`disc.getXPos()` prints `10.0`. It is inherited from Shape through two levels.

items.title: Resolving method calls
notes: The search starts at the **class of the object** (not the variable type), then goes to the **immediate superclass**, and repeats.
It stops when 1) a match is found, or 2) no superclasses remain, and then an error is reported.
The real compiler also checks that the method exists in the declared (reference) type. See Ch5 casting.

items.title: public / private / protected
notes: `public`: accessible anywhere. `private`: only inside that class.
`protected`: the class's methods + **subclass** methods + **any class in the same package**. The slide's slogan is 'Stay in the family'.
'Accessible' means **read and modify**. Protected = `#` in UML.

items.title: Same hierarchy with # (protected) fields
notes: Here Shape's `xPos`/`yPos` are `#` (protected), so Circle and Rectangle can use `xPos` directly by name.
Compare slide 6, where they were `-` (private) and only reachable through getters.
Don't confuse the symbols: `#` = protected, `~` = package, `-` = private, `+` = public.

items.title: Defining a package
notes: A package is a set of classes grouped in the **same directory**. Each file starts with `package packageOne;` before any `import`.
**Non-private** members can be accessed by any class in the same package.

items.title: Package access diagram: who sees iV1-iV4
notes: Class1 has `-iV1` private, `#iV2` protected, `iV3` package (no symbol here), `+iV4` public.
Class2 and Class3 (same package, whether subclass or not): iV2, iV3, iV4. Never iV1.
Class4 (subclass in ANOTHER package): iV2, iV4. Class5 (non-subclass, other package): iV4 only.
So protected wins over package only for subclasses in other packages.

items.title: Visibility table (memorise)
notes: Columns are Class / Package / Subclass / World. public `Y Y Y Y`, protected `Y Y Y N`, not defined (package) `Y Y N N`, private `Y N N N`.
The 'Subclass' column means a subclass in a **different** package. A subclass in the same package already gets package access.
'Not defined' = no modifier = package-private = default.

items.title: Java packages
notes: Packages group classes by **functionality, usability and category**.
Names derive from the internet domain namespace, e.g. `com.foo.users`, `sg.edu.ntu.projects`.
The package namespace is global, so the same class name can exist in different packages.
With no `package` statement, the class goes in the anonymous **default package**.

items.title: Two classes named Deck
notes: `import casino.game.Deck; import star.cruise.Deck;` together is a **compile error** (two single-type imports with the same simple name, verified). The import version is a hidden animation step in the slide text.
Fix: use **fully qualified names**: `casino.game.Deck cards = new casino.game.Deck();`
Typo: the slide's `cards` line is missing its `;`.

items.title: final methods and classes
notes: `final` method: **cannot be overridden** in subclasses.
`final` class: **cannot be a superclass** (no subclasses). Its methods are implicitly final.
The 2 benefits: 1) **security** (behaviour cannot be changed by subclasses), 2) **efficiency** (binding can happen at compile time instead of run time).

items.title: Abstract classes and methods
notes: If a superclass is too general to give meaningful objects, it is an **abstract class** (Abstract Base Class, ABC). It cannot be instantiated.
An abstract method uses the keyword `abstract` and has **no implementation** (it ends with `;`). Subclasses must provide the body.
Moving up the hierarchy = more general (abstraction). Moving down = more specific and concrete.

items.title: UML notation for abstract
notes: Abstract class or method = name in *italics* OR the `{abstract}` constraint.
In the diagram, Figure's `findArea/findPerimeter/print` are italic (abstract). Rectangle and Circle implement them with upright names (concrete).

items.title: abstract class Figure
notes: `public abstract double findArea();` has a semicolon and no `{}`. Writing a body would be a compile error.
An abstract class CAN have fields, constructors and concrete methods (`color`, `Figure(String)`, `getColor()`).
Its constructors run through `super(c)` from subclasses, even though `new Figure()` is illegal.

items.title: FigureApp output
notes: Every double prints with `.0`: `Width = 10.0`, `Area = 100.0`.

items.title: Multiple inheritance (multiple is-a)
notes: Here one subclass has two superclasses: Library (Building, Container), Part-Time Student (Student, Employee), Professor (Researcher, Teacher).
This is allowed in UML/C++, but Java classes CANNOT do it. Interfaces are used instead.

items.title: Interfaces (and the outdated 'only abstract methods')
notes: Java does NOT support multiple inheritance of classes, but a class can implement **multiple interfaces**.
Per the slides: an interface has **only abstract methods + constants (static final)**. An implementing class must implement them **all**, or be declared **abstract**.
Slide outdated: since Java 8, interfaces may have `default` and `static` methods with bodies. Since Java 9, they may also have `private` methods (verified on JDK 17; see Ch10).
Exam: for a Ch3-style 'an interface can only contain…' question, answer per the slide. For modern-Java or default-method questions, answer with real Java.

items.title: IntFigure / Circle implements
notes: Interface methods are implicitly `public abstract`. `void print();` without `abstract` is still abstract.
Implementing methods must be declared `public`. Leaving off `public` is a compile error (weaker access).
Keyword: a class `implements` an interface, while a class `extends` a class.

items.title: Derived interfaces
notes: An interface can be derived from a base interface using `extends BaseInterfaceName` (NOT `implements`).
A concrete class implementing the derived interface must define the methods of **both** the derived AND the base interface.
UML (Ch6): interface-extends-interface is generalisation, drawn as a **solid** line with a hollow triangle.

items.title: IShowablyOrdered extends IOrdered
notes: `Order implements IShowablyOrdered` must implement all 3 methods: `precedes`, `follows` (from IOrdered) and `showOneWhoPrecedes`.
An interface can extend multiple interfaces (`extends A, B`). A class can only extend one class.

items.title: Abstract class vs interface
notes: An abstract class is a real parent (base class). An interface is not a real parent; the slide corrects 'base class' to **type**.
An abstract class can have data members and non-abstract methods. An interface (per the slides) only has constants and abstract methods.
'Constructor?': an abstract class CAN have constructors, but an interface cannot.
A **concrete** class implements all its methods, so it has NO abstract methods.

items.title: Concrete vs abstract vs interface Shape
notes: Concrete: `findArea()` returns a dummy `0`. Abstract: `public abstract double findArea();`. Interface: the methods have no `abstract` keyword but are implicitly abstract.
`String color;` has no modifier, so it is package-private.

items.title: Interface use: INameable
notes: A **dashed** line with a hollow triangle pointing at the `<<interface>>` = realisation (`implements`).
Interfaces give common functionality to possibly **unrelated** classes (Ship, Person, Pet, Building).

items.title: Abstract vs interface table
notes: Abstract class: may have some abstract methods, `protected` members and `static` methods, and both final and non-final fields.
Interface (per the slides): only abstract methods, only `public` methods without implementation, only constants (`static final`).
**Neither** can be instantiated: `new AbstractClass()` and `new Interface()` are both compile errors.

items.title: extends + implements together
notes: Syntax: `class SubClass1 extends SuperClass implements Interface1, Interface2, Interface3`. `extends` comes **before** `implements`.
Diagram: a solid line + hollow triangle to the class (generalisation), and dashed lines + hollow triangles to each interface (realisation).
